chapter: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
title: Learning from 78s then and now; slowing down piano rolls
summary: He contrasts copying arrangements off 78s with modern tape and speakers, and Dance notes Duke learning from slowed piano rolls.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Right! But there was a struggle for competition in the people there, and today's there's none. It's mediocrity involved. [LAUGHS] Although these kids today, they have it made. I don't know... Today... If I copied an arrangement from a record... I had to have a lot of imagination out of a '78, you know. And then, of course, this was in pitch, you know, by the way the turntable... But I mean, in modern technology, in a way, it's more sympathetic to these things, and it's much accurate... I

mean, there's much more accuracy now. For me to sit down and play the piano along with Horowitz and Rubinstein, or Earl Hines, Fats Waller, it's very easy, because all you do is... You have these tremendous speakers, you know; it's right there in the room with you -- you have the actual sound. And the picture is there. You can vary the picture if you want to, from the machine to the piano -- not the piano to the machine. If you want to, you can slow it down, slow a tape down...
I mean, that's what people did in the old days with the piano rolls.
In the old days we didn't have that.
I mean, they slowed them down. That's what Duke said. That's how he learned "Carolina Stomp."
That's true, come to think about it.
